Product Case Study · COGS 127

Helping users make healthier choices without leaving the DoorDash flow

A one-tap Nutrition Mode that overlays dietary risk cues directly onto the DoorDash home feed — so health-conscious users and caregivers can spot high-sodium or high-sugar items before they ever open a menu.

Health UX Accessibility Information Design Decision Support Older Adults

Overview

Food delivery apps are optimized for speed and convenience — not nutrition. For users managing chronic conditions like hypertension or diabetes, that tradeoff creates a real health risk. This project explores what it would look like to layer lightweight nutritional awareness into DoorDash's existing home screen, without disrupting the experience for everyone else.

The core concept: a single toggle in the top navigation bar activates Nutrition Mode. When on, the app surfaces dietary risk indicators — high sodium, high sugar, high saturated fat — directly on restaurant and menu cards. No extra taps required.

Background

Older adults and people managing diet-sensitive conditions increasingly rely on food delivery — especially when mobility is limited or cooking isn't practical. But DoorDash's interface is built around speed: large photos, quick reorder buttons, minimal friction to checkout. Nutrition information, when it exists at all, is buried several taps deep inside individual item pages.

  • Nutritional data is not surfaced during the browse or restaurant selection phase.
  • Users who are hungry or fatigued are least likely to seek out detailed nutrition subpages.
  • Caregivers ordering on behalf of a family member have no way to filter by dietary needs at the top level.
  • DoorDash already collects nutritional data from many restaurant partners — it just isn't shown proactively.

Challenge

How might we make nutrition information actionable at the moment of browsing — without cluttering the interface for users who don't need it, or slowing down DoorDash's convenience-first experience?

The tension: nutrition overlays risk feeling preachy or adding visual noise that imposes healthy choices on people who didn't ask for them. The solution needs to be opt-in, non-judgmental, and fast to activate.

Point of View

Our user research confirmed that the product still feels misaligned with how older adults actually think about food. Many prioritize convenience over hitting nutritional targets — they want to eat, not audit a spreadsheet. That said, users found Nutrition Mode approachable: large text, a clear settings survey, and passive warnings that don't demand attention were all received positively.

Giving users open-ended questions rather than direct inputs made them more comfortable sharing — they didn't feel like their privacy was being stripped away. The challenge ahead is adding enough incentive to choose Nutrition Mode over the default experience.

Key areas for refinement: deeper customization options, a simpler nutrition data layout, and stronger reasons for users to keep Nutrition Mode on rather than treating it as a one-time curiosity.

Approach

  1. Conducted in-depth interviews with two older adult users — one a frequent delivery user managing blood pressure, the other a retired professional with dietary preferences.
  2. Used Zoom screenshare walkthroughs of three prototype variants to observe reactions in real time, with follow-up questions based on hesitations and moments of confusion.
  3. Reviewed CDC and aging research on health communication, decision fatigue, and label design to ground design choices in evidence.
  4. Audited the DoorDash browsing flow to identify the exact points where nutritional context disappears and where it could re-enter with minimal disruption.
  5. Iterated on label language — testing neutral terms like "High sodium" against loaded framings — and on toggle placement to find the lowest-friction entry point.

User Testing

Methodology

We tested three prototype variants with two older adult participants via Zoom screenshare walkthroughs. Each participant was guided through the full UX flow for each prototype and asked to share reactions aloud at each screen. Follow-up interview questions probed hesitations, moments of confusion, and overall preference. Prototypes varied in toggle placement (main screen vs. buried in settings) and survey design (personal data inputs vs. goal-based selection vs. preference sliders).

Participant 1 — Older adult, vegetarian, no specific medical conditions

This participant was candid that Nutrition Mode wasn't designed for someone like her — she eats what she wants — but she could see the value for users who do monitor their diet. Her feedback was detailed and design-critical throughout.

  • Toggle placement: Strongly preferred the toggle on the main screen (Prototype 1). Finding it in settings felt like a barrier.
  • Survey privacy: Disliked fields asking for weight and age specifically — felt unnecessarily personal. More comfortable with preference-based questions.
  • Goal selection: Preferred the "what matters most to you" framing (Prototype 2.2) over the macro/fitness goal screen (Prototype 2.1), which felt more like a gym app than a food app.
  • Drag bar: Liked the strictness slider conceptually — appreciated the customization — but wanted the recommended macros from 2.1 alongside it.
  • Cart screen: The bold "View Nutrition Facts" button made her want to tap it even though she said she didn't care about nutrition. Visibility drives engagement.
  • Overall: Rated Prototype 2.2 as her favorite for the survey experience, but agreed with Prototype 1 on toggle placement.

Participant 2 — Rick Lopez, 77, retired bank manager, managing blood pressure

Rick had no prior awareness that nutrition information existed anywhere in DoorDash. That made him an ideal test participant — he represented a user with genuine unmet needs, not someone who had already found a workaround.

  • Toggle placement: Responded positively to the toggle on the main screen — said he would actually see it there. When moved to settings in Prototype 2, he had to be guided to it and called it "extra work."
  • Survey privacy: Raised concern about personal data fields — specifically worried that sharing weight and age could affect his insurance. Relaxed once questions shifted to preferences rather than personal metrics.
  • Inline warnings: Noticed the high-sodium warning on the item screen immediately without being prompted. Said "yeah, I'd see that" — confirming that passive, ambient cues work for this user group.
  • Macro framing: The goal-selection screen in Prototype 2.1 felt unfamiliar — he wasn't used to thinking about food in terms of macros or fitness goals. Said it felt more like a gym app.
  • Strictness slider: Confused by the drag bar — wasn't sure what he was adjusting or what the numbers meant.
  • Key insight: "I want to be informed, not instructed." Warnings that appear on their own are welcome. Anything that requires extra effort before ordering will get skipped.
  • Overall: Preferred Prototype 1 for toggle visibility and inline warnings. Preferred Prototype 2.2's survey page over 2.1's goal-based screen.

Synthesis

Both participants converged on the same core finding: accessibility of the toggle and passivity of the warnings are the most critical design decisions. Users want nutritional awareness to come to them, not the other way around. The survey is a meaningful touchpoint, but only when it asks about preferences rather than personal data. The drag-bar customization, while conceptually appealing, introduced more confusion than it resolved for this age group.

For DoorDash's business goals, this matters: if Nutrition Mode is too hard to find or activate, adoption stalls and the feature provides no value. If it's passive and well-placed, it becomes a genuine differentiator for health-conscious users without disrupting anyone else's flow.

Before & After Stories

The following screens show the key changes introduced by Nutrition Mode. Each annotation explains what changed, why it changed, and how it connects to the user testing findings above.

1 — The Nutrition Mode Toggle

The most debated design decision was where to put the toggle. Both participants confirmed what the research suggested: if it's in settings, it gets skipped. Placing it in the top navigation bar — alongside the profile, notifications, and cart icons — makes it part of the primary UI that users scan on every visit.

Before Toggle is off (grey). The home feed looks exactly like the standard DoorDash experience — no nutrition cues, no visual change.
  • No nutrition context visible at any point in the browse flow
  • Users like Rick had no idea nutrition data existed in the app
After Toggle is on (red). The same home screen now carries nutrition risk cues inline — no navigation required to activate.
  • Toggle placed in primary nav — visible on every home screen visit
  • Opt-in by default: zero change for users who don't want it
  • Rick noted he would "actually see it there" vs. a settings menu

2 — The Onboarding Survey & Preference Flow

Once Nutrition Mode is activated, users are guided through a short onboarding flow to personalize their experience. Testing revealed a clear hierarchy of what works and what creates friction across the three prototype variants.

Screen 1 — Home (toggle off)

Starting state. No nutrition layer active. Familiar DoorDash layout preserved.

Screen 2 — "Tell us what matters most"

Goal-selection screen with specific targets (lose weight, build muscle, eat cleaner). Both participants preferred this framing over screens that asked for personal data like age or weight. The goal-based approach feels empowering rather than clinical.

⚠ Friction point: the macro/fitness goal framing felt more like a gym app than a food app to Rick. Needs softer language for older adults.

Screen 3 — Smart Recommendations

Auto-generated macro thresholds based on selected goal (sodium, added sugars, saturated fat, macros) with source citations (AHA, WHO, USDA). Participant 1 liked seeing recommended values. Reduces cognitive load — users don't need to know their own thresholds.

Screen 4 — "How strict for each?"

Per-nutrient strictness sliders with categories: Free, Limit, Avoid, Allergic. Conceptually appealing — both participants liked the idea of customization — but Rick found the slider interaction confusing and wasn't sure what adjusting it meant in practice. Needs clearer labels or a simpler interaction model for older users.

Learnings & Reflections

The biggest insight from this project was how much placement and passivity determine whether a health feature gets used at all. Nutritional data buried in a submenu might as well not exist for a tired or hungry user making a quick dinner decision. Both participants confirmed this independently: Rick didn't know DoorDash had nutrition data; Participant 1 said she wouldn't go looking for it but would notice it if it appeared on its own.

The survey findings reinforced a second principle: ask for preferences, not personal data. Questions about goals and dietary values felt comfortable and relevant. Questions about age and weight felt invasive — and for Rick, raised real-world concerns about insurance implications. The difference between a helpful onboarding flow and a privacy violation can come down to a single field.

The strictness slider is the open design question. It tests well conceptually — users understand why it exists — but fails in execution for older adults who aren't familiar with macro-level nutrition thinking. A future iteration might replace the slider with plain-language options (e.g., "Show me a heads-up" vs. "Hide this from my feed") that achieve the same personalization without requiring nutritional literacy.

If this concept moved forward, next steps would include broader testing across more diverse age groups and health contexts, working with restaurant partners to ensure nutritional data coverage, and exploring how the overlay behaves on search results, past orders, and favorites — not just the home feed.
